Induction Machine Fundamentals: Slip, Equivalent Circuit, Power Flow and Torque (Ch7)

Why this matters in the exam: Q3 of every final is “AC and Induction Machines” (20 marks). After the 6-mark part (a) on Ch4–5 basics (pack M6), the rest is Ch7. Jun23 Q3b (5 marks) is induction torque–speed and . Jun24 Q3b (4 marks) is the parameter tests and Jun24 Q3c (10 marks) is a full equivalent-circuit calculation: slip, , input current, , and torque. Ch7 was not in the mid-semester test or quiz, and the files give only numerical answers for it. So this is about 14–15 marks you have never practised under time pressure. Every one of them uses the tools in this pack.

Scope: this pack covers construction, slip, the equivalent circuit, power flow and torque. Pack M6 covers and Jun23 Q3a (ideal efficiency). Pack M8 covers the no-load and blocked-rotor tests, the slip for maximum torque, and generator mode (Jun24 Q3c is generator mode, so it lives there, but its method is Type C below).

1. The core ideas

1.1 Construction and operation (Lecture 7.1)

  • Stator: a three-phase winding in slots of a laminated iron core. The three-phase supply produces a magnetic field of constant magnitude rotating at synchronous speed .
  • Rotor: a short-circuited three-phase winding in a laminated core. The airgap is as small as possible (about 0.5 mm).
  • Operation: the rotor sees the field moving past it at the slip speed . This induces rotor voltages () and, because the rotor is short-circuited, rotor currents. These currents interact with the field to give force and so torque. To a first approximation torque is proportional to slip speed. At nothing is induced, so the torque is zero.
  • Motoring when . Generating when .
  • Mechanical analogy (PQ 7.2): synchronous machine = two disks joined by a spring (same speed, twist angle sets torque). Induction machine = two disks in a viscous fluid (torque proportional to the speed difference).
Squirrel-cage rotor Wound rotor
Rotor winding solid bars (normally cast aluminium) shorted at both ends by end-rings three-phase winding brought out to slip-rings
fixed can be increased with an external three-phase resistor (pack M8)
Use by far the most common. Cheap, robust where starting torque or speed must be adjusted
Other bars are skewed to run more smoothly

Advantages of induction motors (PQ 7.1b): self-starting, lowest cost, wide range of sizes (100 W to 10 MW), high efficiency, reliable, nearly constant speed.

1.3 The per-phase equivalent circuit (Lecture 7.4)

An induction machine is a rotating transformer with a short-circuited secondary. Referring the rotor to the stator (in turns and in frequency) turns the real rotor (frequency , resistance , reactance ) into a circuit at frequency with constant and a variable effective rotor resistance .

Full equivalent circuit (Lecture 7.4.3): → → → node → shunt → → .

Simplified equivalent circuit (Lecture 7.4.4), which the course uses for all calculations:

 I1 -->        I2' -->
 o-----+--------+---- R1 ---- jX ---- R2'/s ----+
       |        |    (jX = jX1 + jX2')           |
  V1   RC      jXM                               |    : airgap is between
       |        |                                |    : jX and R2'/s
 o-----+--------+--------------------------------+
     IM = V1/RC + V1/(jXM)
  • The shunt branch () moves to the supply terminals, so it sees .
  • The series branch is , with . Unlike the transformer, and are not combined, because only is “in the rotor”.
  • , with .

Differences from a transformer (PQ 7.10c): the secondary is short-circuited, the effective rotor resistance varies with slip, and the magnetising current is much larger (25–60 % of rated current versus about 1 %) because of the airgap.

Ideal efficiency. Since and :

This counts only the rotor copper loss. Stator copper, iron and friction losses make the real efficiency lower (PQ 7.11d). The worked Jun23 Q3a use is in pack M6.

1.5 Torque (Lecture 7.5.4–7.5.5)

Like the fluid coupling, the torque is the same on both “disks”, which turn at (field) and (rotor):

Substituting from the simplified circuit gives the course torque formula (formula sheet, Lecture 7.5.5):

  • is the phase voltage. The shunt branch does not appear, because it sits across the supply and does not change .
  • Use (synchronous, rad/s), not the rotor speed.
  • At a fixed slip, : torque is very sensitive to supply voltage.
  • Small slip: dominates, so , i.e.  (the linear region of pack M6). Large slip: dominates, so . The peak in between is the pull-out torque (typically about 2× rated). Finding it is pack M8.

Set up for Example 2: check the operating point sits near 960 rpm (s = 0.04), then drop V by 10 % and watch the slip rise to hold the same torque.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Putting the line voltage into a star-connected circuit. For a 415 V star motor, V. For delta, . Using the wrong one gets the torque wrong by a factor of 3.
  • Using instead of in or in the torque formula. goes with , and goes with .
  • Rotor copper loss as . That is . Rotor Cu loss is .
  • Calling the output. The output is .
  • Adding and as magnitudes. They are phasors about 75° apart. Convert to rectangular first.
  • Using in the stator copper loss in the simplified circuit. is in the series branch, so it carries (Lecture 7.5.1).
  • Rounding slip early. instead of 0.02222 changes by 11 %.
  • Rotor frequency = supply frequency. It is , a few Hz at rated speed.

PQ 7.1 (practice questions). Answer the following questions about induction machines.

  1. The rotor winding of an induction machine consists of ________.
  2. List three advantages of induction motors.
  3. The most common type of induction motor rotor is called the ________ rotor. The rotor winding in this rotor normally consists of ________ bars.
  4. To a first approximation the torque of an induction machine is directly proportional to ________.
  5. An induction machine acts a generator when the rotor speed is ________ than the synchronous speed. It acts as a motor when the rotor speed is ________ than the synchronous speed.
  6. The equivalent circuit of an induction machine is similar to that of a ________.
  7. In an induction machine equivalent circuit, the power conversion between electrical and mechanical power is modelled by a ________.
  8. What is the starting and pull-out torque?
Solution
  1. A short-circuited three-phase winding.
  2. Any three of: low cost, self-starting, high efficiency, reliable, available in a wide range of sizes.
  3. Squirrel-cage rotor. The bars are normally aluminium.
  4. The slip speed .
  5. Generator when the rotor speed is greater than . Motor when it is less.
  6. A transformer (with a short-circuited secondary).
  7. A resistor: .
  8. Starting torque is the torque at zero speed (). Pull-out torque is the maximum torque the motor can produce at any speed.

PQ 7.2 (practice questions). There are two common mechanical analogies used to describe the operation of synchronous and induction machines. They are both based on modelling the stator magnetic field and the rotor as rotating disks where the stator magnetic field is rotating at synchronous speed. Using the templates below, illustrate these analogies. Label any additional elements added to the figures. No explanation of the analogies are required.

Solution
  • Synchronous machine: join the disks with a spring. Both turn at exactly . The twist of the spring (the rotor angle) sets the torque.
  • Induction machine: put a viscous fluid between the disks. The rotor disk lags the field disk. The torque is proportional to the speed difference (slip speed). Power flows from the faster disk to the slower one.

PQ 7.3 (practice questions). Calculate the synchronous speed (in rpm) for the following AC machines:

  1. 4 pole, 50 Hz (b) 8 pole, 60 Hz (c) 2 pole, 50 Hz (d) 4 pole, 800 Hz (e) 24 pole, 50 Hz
Solution

:

  1. 1500 rpm. (b) 900 rpm. (c) 3000 rpm. (d) 24 000 rpm. (e) 250 rpm.

PQ 7.4 (practice questions). Calculate the most likely number of poles and supply frequency for motors with the following synchronous speeds.

  1. 1,500 rpm (b) 1800 rpm (c) 750 rpm (d) 1,200 rpm (e) 360 rpm (f) 150 rpm
Solution

Try and Hz in poles and keep the answer that is an even integer:

  1. 1500 rpm: 50 Hz gives 4 (60 Hz gives 4.8). 4 poles, 50 Hz.
  2. 1800 rpm: 60 Hz gives 4 poles, 60 Hz.
  3. 750 rpm: 50 Hz gives 8 poles, 50 Hz (60 Hz gives 9.6).
  4. 1200 rpm: 60 Hz gives 6 poles, 60 Hz (50 Hz gives 5, which is odd).
  5. 360 rpm: 60 Hz gives 20 poles, 60 Hz (50 Hz gives 16.67).
  6. 150 rpm: 40 poles at 50 Hz or 48 poles at 60 Hz. Both are valid.

PQ 7.6 (practice questions). Consider a 7.5 kW, 2910 rpm three-phase 50Hz induction machine operating at rated voltage. Refer to Section 7.2 of your notes if you have difficulty with this.

  1. Calculate its synchronous speed in rpm and hence the rated slip speed in rpm.
  2. The machine is running at no-load, calculate its operating speed in rpm.
  3. At what speed does rated output torque occur at? Calculate the rated output torque.
  4. Calculate the rated operating speed as a percentage of the no load operating speed. Is the description of induction machines as almost fixed speed machines valid?
  5. Calculate the speed (in rpm) at which the motor operates with half rated output torque.
  6. Calculate the output power corresponding to part (e). Express this as a percentage of rated output power. Why is this not exactly half the rated output power?
  7. Calculate the operating speed corresponding to a load of 20 Nm.
  8. The machine is driven at 3070 rpm. Is the machine acting as a motor or generator? Calculate the output torque.
Solution

Use the linear torque–speed line through and (Lecture 7.2.2), so .

  1. , so , 3000 rpm. Rated slip speed 90 rpm.

  2. At no load τ = 0, so slip speed = 0 and 3000 rpm (ideally).

  3. Rated torque occurs at rated speed, 2910 rpm.

  4. 97 %. Yes: the speed drops only 3 % from no load to full load, so “almost fixed speed” is fair.

  5. Half torque means half the slip speed, 45 rpm. 2955 rpm.

  6. 3.808 kW, which is 50.77 % of rated. It is more than half because the speed (2955 rpm) is higher than rated speed. In fact .

Disagreement with the PQ answer: the PQ gives 3.801 kW and 50.68 %. Those numbers are , i.e. the answer used 2950 rpm instead of its own 2955 rpm from part (e). With 2955 rpm the correct values are 3.808 kW and 50.77 %. The explanation (higher speed) is the same.

  1. Slip speed rpm, so 2927 rpm.

  2. 3070 rpm is above , so it is a generator. Slip speed rpm. The negative sign means the shaft drives the machine.

  2. The difference between synchronous speed and rotor speed, .

    1. Low slip: . (ii) High slip: .

INDUCTION MACHINE FUNDAMENTALS (Ch7)
n_S = 60f/p (p = pole PAIRS) = 120f/poles     w_S = 2*pi*n_S/60
s = (n_S - n)/n_S      n = (1-s) n_S      f2 = s f      slip speed = n_S - n
s=1 standstill (f2=f), s=0 sync (R2'/s = inf), s<0 generator (R2'/s < 0)
Keep s to 4 s.f.

SIMPLIFIED CCT (per phase):  V1 || (RC // jXM)  then  R1 + jX + R2'/s,  X = X1 + X2'
  star: V1 = VL/sqrt3, I1 = IL     delta: V1 = VL, IL = sqrt3 I1     V1 at 0 deg
  I2' = V1/(R1 + R2'/s + jX)    IM = V1/RC - jV1/XM    I1 = I2' + IM  (rectangular!)
R2'/s = R2' (heat) + R2'(1-s)/s (mech power)

POWER FLOW (3-ph totals)
  P_IN = 3 V1 I1 cos(phi)
  - stator Cu 3 I2'^2 R1   - iron 3 V1^2/RC
  = P_AG = 3 I2'^2 R2'/s = τ w_S
  rotor Cu = 3 I2'^2 R2' = s P_AG      P_M = (1-s) P_AG = τ w
  ideal eta <= 1 - s = n/n_S          eta = P_M/P_IN

TORQUE   τ = P_AG/w_S = P_M/w = 3 I2'^2 R2'/(s w_S)
  τ = 3 V1^2 (R2'/s) / { w_S [ (R1 + R2'/s)^2 + (X1+X2')^2 ] }    (V1 = PHASE V)
  τ ~ V1^2 at fixed s;  low s: τ ~ s;  high s: τ ~ 1/s

TYPE C STEPS: V1 -> n_S, s, R2'/s -> draw cct -> I2' -> IM -> I1, pf -> P_IN
             -> P_AG -> τ = P_AG/w_S (check formula) -> P_M -> eta (check loss sum)
